summary: For 5–7 year olds learning what living things need to survive. The core idea is that a 'need' is defined by what happens when it is withheld: observing a visible consequence (a wilting plant) anchors the concept. Children build animal needs from their own body experience (hunger, thirst, breathing), then compare the animal list (needs food it cannot make) with the plant list (needs light and makes its own food), seeding the later idea that animals depend on plants. Keep air and warmth concrete and observational; avoid mechanism (photosynthesis, gas exchange) which belongs to later key stages.
misconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil' — treating soil/water as food and missing that plants make food from light.
Assuming plants and animals need the SAME things (e.g. that plants need to be 'fed' food, or that animals photosynthesise).
Thinking a need is optional or cosmetic rather than survival-critical, because consequences are slow and unseen.
Confusing 'want' with 'need' (a pet 'needs' a toy) — not distinguishing survival needs from comforts.

activities.title: Side-by-side windowsill care bench
steps: Set up (or run a model of) two living things to care for: a bean plant in a pot and a small animal such as a hamster in a hutch.

Choose what to provide to each from a shared set of supplies: a watering can, a lamp for light, air, warmth, and a food bowl. With a real hamster, always give it everything it needs; only leave needs out in the model.
Give the plant water but leave it in the dark, and watch over time (days, or time-compressed in a model) to see it stay alive but grow pale and leggy.
Notice that the plant has NO food bowl and still grows, while the animal must be fed — then explain why the two lists differ.
Rescue a wilting or pale plant by restoring the one missing need, and describe what changed.
activities.insight: A need is proven by its consequence: withhold it and the living thing visibly suffers. Plants and animals need different things — plants need light and make their own food, animals cannot make food and must be fed.

activities.title: Classroom split-plant fair test over a week
steps: Plant two identical seedlings and give both equal water.
Place one in a bright spot and cover the other with a lightproof box (or put it in a dark cupboard) in the same room, keeping water, pot, soil and temperature as similar as possible.
Before the week passes, predict whether the dark seedling will grow as healthily (green and sturdy) as the light one, and say WHY. Remember a plant in the dark may grow taller but pale and floppy.
Observe both plants over several days and record what changes.
Compare the result to the prediction and state which need was missing from the weaker plant.
activities.insight: Changing only one variable (light) while keeping water, temperature and everything else as similar as possible shows that light is a genuine need for healthy growth: water alone is not enough.

activities.title: Name the needs and what uses them
steps: Look at a plant and an animal and name each basic need aloud: for the plant — water, light, air, suitable temperature; for the animal — water, food, air, shelter/warmth.
Pair each need with the part or behaviour that uses it, e.g. roots take up water, leaves use light, the animal's mouth takes in food.
For each need, say what the living thing would look like if that need were missing (e.g. 'no water → wilts', 'no light → pale', 'no food → weak').
activities.insight: Each need is linked to a part or behaviour of the organism and to a specific consequence if it is missing.

activities.title: Sort and match: plant needs, animal needs, both
steps: Sort need cards into three groups: 'plant needs', 'animal needs', and 'both'.
Match each 'need' card to a 'consequence of lacking it' card (e.g. no water → wilts; no food → weak; no light → pale).
Consider the common wrong idea that 'plants get their food from the soil' and explain why it is incorrect.
Optionally use a 'how much water' slider to show that too little or too much is a problem.
activities.insight: The two need-lists overlap (water, air, suitable temperature/warmth) but differ in key ways (plants need light and make their own food; animals need food they cannot make).

activities.title: Talk in-role with a thirsty plant or hungry pet
steps: Take part in a conversation where a plant or animal gives graded hints about how it feels (e.g. 'my leaves are drooping...', 'I feel hungry...').
Infer which need is missing from the hints and say what to provide.
Explain, for a plant, why you would NOT offer it food, and for an animal why you would.
Extend the pattern to other animals: say what a goldfish would be missing if it were taken out of the water, and point out that a worm in the soil still needs air.
Talk about whether sleeping is a need that all living things share — note that an animal such as the hamster sleeps but a plant does not, so sleeping is not a universal survival need.
activities.insight: Caring reasoning — matching a described symptom to the missing need — reinforces that each need has a felt consequence, that the same pattern holds across different animals, and that plant and animal needs differ, with some human/animal behaviours (like sleeping) not being universal needs.

checkQuestion: A plant is watered every day but kept in a dark cupboard with the door shut. It's getting plenty of water — so will it grow well, or is it missing something it needs? Explain what will happen and why.
checkAnswer: It won't grow well — it's missing light. Plants need light (as well as water, air and a suitable temperature); without light the plant goes pale, weak and eventually dies, because water alone isn't enough. Living things suffer if any one of their basic needs is missing.
